title: Inclusion and equality of enumerable sets

based_on.title: Computability theory
based_on.pages: Version 2024-02-25; §17.2 Exercise 17.6, p.72; inclusion classification corrected to Pi2

based_on.title: 13. Cubbyhole Mathematics
based_on.pages: Proposition 3, Exercise 2, and the equality upper-bound example

summary: Classify inclusion and equality of enumerable domains as complete universal second-level problems, and their failures as complete existential second-level problems.
abstract: Two programs may halt on exactly the same inputs while returning different outputs. Comparing their domains asks whether one enumerable set is contained in another, or whether the two sets agree. A finite enumeration can show that an input has appeared, but its current absence from the other enumeration may disappear later. This asymmetry gives inclusion and equality their universal second-level descriptions in the arithmetical hierarchy. Both descriptions are exact: comparing a program's domain with the whole natural numbers already tests totality, a complete problem at that level. Taking complements classifies failure of inclusion and inequality at the existential second level. Explicit translations establish these lower bounds, while finite examples separate domain comparison from equality of the functions computed by the programs.
